intro.title: WarShip Project Overview
intro.desc: This page presents the core implementation of my WarShip project through gameplay videos and source snippets, including scene flow, board logic, combat effects, and resource systems.

text: Core Gameplay Implementation
The core loop is strictly turn-based with alternating players. At the start of each turn, available resources are recalculated from fleet state (Missile / Attack / Skill counts).

All actions in a turn must stay within those resource limits. Each action consumes its quota immediately. When resources are exhausted, or the player ends the turn manually, control switches to Next Player.
The battlefield is a 20x20 TileBoard. Each Tile stores grid state (empty, hit, unexplored, etc.) plus an optional Ship* reference, enabling fast lookup for hit checks and rendering.
Main Modules and Features

Game Preparation: After entering the game, players first go to the shop scene. Hovering ships shows detailed info. Clicking a ship triggers ship_factory to create the ship instance and completes the purchase by deducting current player coins.

Ships can be dragged onto the board. Before placement, boundary and overlap validation is performed. Invalid positions are reverted to the last valid state. A reset button clears the board and restores initial setup.
Before Match Start: After both players finish shopping and placement, the game performs a pre-check of each player's ship list and removes ships that were not actually placed on the board.
Gameplay Flow: For balance, the starting player cannot cast skills on the first move and can only use normal attacks. The selected attack target is validated before firing.
When a player attempts a skill, legality is checked at the skill center point; out-of-bounds affected cells are ignored safely.

After projectile arrival, the target tile state is evaluated and matching effects/sounds are played. Repeated hits on non-sunk ships play a generic explosion without applying extra damage; repeated hits on sunk positions play a seabed-style explosion sound.
A ship is marked sunk when received hits are greater than or equal to its HP + shield value.

Skill System: Different ship classes have different skills to increase strategic variety. Skills mainly include burst attack and detection, plus special ship-only abilities such as anti-detection and repair reinforcement.
Game End: The match ends when all ships of either player are marked as sunk, then transitions to the settlement scene.
Implementation Highlights and Technical Details:
Scene Architecture (SceneManager + ScenePool):
A unified scene manager dispatches Menu / Shop / Game / Settlement scenes, each following enter/update/render/exit lifecycle hooks.
ScenePool reuses scene instances to avoid frequent create/destroy churn, reducing state confusion and resource leaks while making scene switching easier to maintain.
Input and Logic Decoupling (Event Dispatch + UI Callback):
SDL events are normalized in the input layer. UI components (such as Button) bind callbacks to domain actions, enforcing the rule: UI triggers intent, gameplay rules execute logic.
This avoids UI code mutating board data directly and makes it easier to extend future input methods like shortcuts and gesture-like controls.
Centralized Ship Creation (ShipFactory):
Different ship types are consistently constructed and initialized through ShipFactory, so buy/spawn flows do not depend on concrete class names.
Adding a new ship type only requires extending the type definition and factory branch, minimizing invasive changes to upper-layer game flow.
Board Data Structure (20x20 TileBoard + Tile State):
The core battlefield uses a 20x20 TileBoard. Each Tile tracks state (visible/hit/unexplored, etc.) and an optional Ship* reference.
Attack and skill resolution are board-centric with legality checks and state updates, while rendering only reflects state, keeping rules and presentation separated.
Attack Presentation -> Result Commit (Bullet / Effect Callback + Prototype Cloning):
Projectile flight, arrival, effects, and audio are treated as a presentation pipeline. Settlement is triggered by callbacks when Bullet arrives or when a key Effect playback point is reached.
This makes rule updates happen at synchronized presentation checkpoints, avoiding hard-coded delays and visual-state desync.
The effect system uses a template + clone reuse model. EffectManager pre-registers effect templates (for example Explosion / Splash).
Instead of constructing concrete effects directly at runtime, it calls Effect::clone() to duplicate from templates.

The cloned instance is then configured with target position/playback params and queued into manager update/render lists. This avoids repeated loading and repetitive initialization while keeping new effects easy to add.
Attack Resolution Chain (Input -> Presentation -> Commit):
The project decouples target selection from board data mutation. Attack flow advances through fixed stages to keep visual feedback and final state consistent:
1) Target Preview: after selecting a target, run legality checks first; if valid, only update selection state and preview effects, without mutating hit data.
2) Bullet Spawn: once target validity is confirmed, BulletManager spawns the projectile and advances flight updates over time (position/animation), starting the presentation phase.
3) On Arrive: when the bullet reaches target tile, the arrival callback evaluates tile state (hit/miss/repeat-hit) and selects corresponding feedback type.

4) Effect Playback: hits play explosion effects; misses play splash effects; repeat hits choose different sounds depending on whether the ship is already sunk. EffectManager owns effect lifecycle and playback callbacks.

5) State Commit: at bullet-arrival or key effect-sync/end points, update tile visibility/hit states and ship hit/sunk markers (hits >= HP + shield), ensuring presentation and data stay strictly aligned.
Resource and Performance Optimization (Resource Cache + Text Texture Cache + Atlas Animation):
ResourcesManager centralizes load/cache for textures, fonts, and sounds. Resource references are reused across scene switches to avoid duplicate loading.
Frequently used UI text is texture-cached (TxtTextureManager) to reduce repeated text texture generation overhead.
Animation resources are organized through Atlas/Animation for unified sprite-sheet playback control, improving rhythm consistency and reuse for units/effects.
Current Limitations

Singleton implementations are not thread-safe. Resource-loading paths still contain too much hard-coded logic and could be generalized with iterative path assembly. Skill-consumption logic is currently handled in scene layer rather than inside Player. A unified GameObject abstraction is also worth introducing for global object management.
Future Plan

The project paused mainly because gameplay depth under the current skill system is limited. Many matches quickly become both sides dumping all skills early, then devolving into simple A-to-A exchanges. I tried increasing ammo after turn 15 to shorten long rounds, but the gain was limited and overall experience remained weak.

Next, I plan to refactor the skill module with a cooldown system so skills become recoverable turn-based resources rather than one-shot consumables. Skill availability and cadence will differ by ship type (some available at start, others unlocked at specific turns), and attack/skill resource logic will be further tuned.
I also plan to add an AI opponent with a state-machine flow: random search -> target acquired -> focused sinking attempt, and later explore online multiplayer support.
